newsitem.title: USA: Dollar ends mixed after volatile trading session.
newsitem.headline: Dollar ends mixed after volatile trading session.

text.p: The dollar ended mixed against European currencies Friday but reached a 33-month high against the Japanese yen after a roller-coaster session.

Trading centred on the German mark, which gyrated after several German officials gave conflicting views on the outlook for domestic interest rates, and the British pound, which rallied on strong economic performance in Britain.
Three officials of the German central bank said they did not expect to see lower German interest rates ahead, but two of the officials expressed hope that rate cuts were still possible.
The dollar climbed against the mark on the news, since lower German rates would enhance the relative value of assets priced in dollars.
But release of a radio interview with Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer in which he asserted Germany's economy would grow through 1997 without a rate cut sent the mark soaring against the dollar.

"There were a number of comments out of German authorities as to the interest rate picture and the dollar reacted to every single one of them," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan New York.

The dollar closed at 1.5200 marks, up from 1.5177 late Thursday, but below the session high at 1.5263. Against the yen, the dollar finished at 113.42, its highest close since January 1994, up from 112.81.

The British pound rose to $1.6048 from 1.5945 late Thursday after reaching a 15-month peak earlier in the session. The dollar rose to 1.2617 Swiss francs from 1.2555, but fell to Canadian $1.3449 from C$1.3457.
Sterling rallied on a report that the British economy grew 0.8 percent in the third quarter, exceeding expectations.
"Britain's economy looks good and people are expecting higher interest rates there," said Dominick Presser, chief dealer at Dresdner Bank in New York.
The dollar benefited from solid U.S. economic data during New York trading, dealers said.
The Commerce Department reported U.S. durable goods orders rose a robust 4.6 percent in September and the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index rose faster than expected.
"Those reports need to be picked apart, but they seemed to indicate reasonable growth," said Pettit.
The dollar also continued to rally against the yen, boosted by Japanese investors selling yen to invest in higher-yielding overseas markets.
But the U.S. unit may have reached a near-term peak as it approaches 113.60 yen, the January 1994 high, which dealers said is a key technical level.
"The dollar has been grinding higher against the yen, and it should continue to do so," said Presser.
